spans.text: RV32 bare-metal carrier: a memory-mapped mailbox (design, R5; not built)
Ruled 2026-09-04 with the R5 adjudication: the RV32

— chosen so that the in-repo interpreter and QEMU user-mode both service the same image — and is not the canonical bare-metal carrier. This document is the carrier that is. Nothing here is implemented; nothing here changes what a transition means.
1. What a carrier is, and is not

The 48-byte command frame and the 32-byte outcome frame are the ABI. A carrier moves those bytes and says when they are ready. It does not decide anything: admission does (R0.4.6/R0.4.7), and evidence egress is an orthogonal obligation with its own channel (R3). A carrier that could refuse a transition, or that carried evidence in the response, would be a semantic change and is out of scope by construction.
A fixed block of memory at a link-time address (
in the RAM region so the same 64 KiB map governs it), owned half by the host and half by the floor:

blocks.text:
offset  size  field             writer   meaning
0       4     magic             host     "CDMB" — the host has mapped the block
4       4     version           host     carrier version, 1
8       4     command_status    host→floor→host
                                  0 EMPTY   host may write command[]
                                  1 READY   host has written a complete 48-byte command; floor may consume
                                  2 TAKEN   floor has copied command[] out; host may write the next
16      48    command           host     one COMMAND frame, byte-for-byte the fd-0 frame
64      4     response_status   floor→host→floor
                                  0 EMPTY   floor may write response[]
                                  1 READY   floor has written a complete 32-byte outcome; host may read
                                  2 TAKEN   host has copied response[] out; floor may write the next
80      32    response          floor    one OUTCOME frame, byte-for-byte the fd-1 frame
112     4     control           host     bit 0 STOP — the floor exits its loop at the next EMPTY
116     4     exit_code         floor    written once, when the floor leaves the loop
120     4     fault             floor    0, or a fault code if the floor panicked (the panic handler writes it)
124     4     reserved

spans.text: 128 bytes. Every status field is a whole aligned word written with a single

after the payload it announces (release order: payload, then status); the reader polls the status word and reads the payload after seeing it. On a single hart with no caches this is sufficient; on anything else a
sits between the payload and the status store (

blocks.text:
loop:
    wait until command_status == READY        (poll; wfi where the target has it)
    copy command[48] out                      (the same read_exact the hostcall lowering has, over memory)
    command_status = TAKEN                    (release)
    dispatch                                  (unchanged)
    wait until response_status != READY       (the host has drained the previous outcome)
    write response[32]; response_status = READY
    if control & STOP: exit_code = 0; break

spans.text: for any fd other than 1 returns EBADF, as the hostcall one does: evidence egress does not ride this mailbox.
R3's ruling stands: egress exports truth without gaining authority over it, and a committed transition whose evidence cannot cross the boundary poisons the floor. On this carrier that boundary is a
block — an egress ring of N × 52-byte

frames with a producer index the floor owns and a consumer index the host owns — so that command latency never couples to evidence throughput (the same reason fd 3 is not fd 1). A full ring is the poison condition, exactly as EAGAIN/ENOTCONN is on Linux. Not designed further here.

blocks.text:
QEMU virt machine     the block in DRAM; the host side is a QEMU test device or a second hart
ESP32-P4              shared SRAM between the HP core running the floor and the host core
FPGA                  a BRAM with the host side on the fabric; status words become ready/valid handshakes
CD1 hardware queue    the same 128-byte contract as a register file
